intro: The relative clause you already know, consolidated and stretched. The pronoun is still der, die, das, die by gender and number; nominative when it is the subject of its clause, accusative (den) when it is the object; comma before, verb at the end. What is new here is where the clause can sit and what can be inside it. It can interrupt the main sentence: Die Frau, die Deutsch spricht, ist nett — two commas, and the main verb waits until the clause is closed. It can contain a Perfekt or a modal: das Handy, das ich gestern gekauft habe; der Film, den wir sehen wollen. And the relative pronoun is chosen only by its role inside its own clause, never by the noun's role outside it: Ich kenne den Mann, der dort steht — den in the main clause, der in the relative clause, because there he is the subject.
tips[0].title: Case from inside the clause, never from outside
tips[0].text: Ich kenne den Mann, der dort steht (he stands → Nom). Der Mann, den ich kenne, wohnt hier (I know him → Akk). The noun's case in the main sentence is irrelevant.
tips[0].trap: English 'that' does not change, so learners copy the main-clause case. Ask only: inside the relative clause, is it doing the verb (der) or receiving it (den)?
tips[0].check.why: Inside the relative clause the technician does the repairing, so he is the subject: der, even though the main clause has den Techniker.
tips[1].title: The clause in the middle: two commas, main verb waits
tips[1].text: Die Frau, | die Deutsch spricht, | ist nett. Der Film, | den wir sehen wollen, | läuft um acht. Close the relative clause with its verb, then continue the main clause immediately with its verb.
tips[1].check.why: A relative clause in the middle has a comma on both sides and its verb at the end; the main verb kommt follows straight after the second comma.
tips[2].title: Perfekt and modals inside: helper last
tips[2].text: …, das ich gekauft habe · …, den wir sehen wollen · …, die ich einladen möchte. The relative clause is a subordinate clause; everything obeys the verb-last rule.
tips[2].check.why: In the relative clause the conjugated modal goes last, after the infinitive: die wir mieten wollen.
tips[3].title: Nom = article, Akk = article except den
tips[3].text: der die das die / den die das die. Say it as a rhythm. Dative and genitive relatives (dem, denen, dessen) are the next quiz.
tips[3].check.why: Only the masculine changes in the accusative (den); neuter stays das: das Buch, das ich lese.
remember[0]: Choose der/den by the pronoun's job inside its clause.
remember[1]: Middle clause = two commas, and the main verb comes right after the second.
mistakes[0].why: Inside the clause he is the subject: der.
mistakes[1].why: A middle relative clause needs a closing comma.
hook: Describe people and things in one flowing sentence – der Kollege, der neben mir sitzt – even with the clause in the middle.
recall.known: From "Relativsätze: der, die, das (Nom/Akk)": the pronoun is the article, only den is new.
recall.today: The clause in the middle of a sentence, and Perfekt or a modal inside it.
